title: Dealing with Contention
summary: Decide how two users fighting over the same row should be resolved.
keyPoints: Contention is a correctness problem before it is a performance problem.
A conditional single-row update is the simplest protection against lost updates.
Unique constraints encode one-of-a-kind invariants without application-level locks.
Pessimistic locking suits likely conflicts; optimistic version checks suit rare ones.
A distributed lock needs a fencing token to remain safe after a lease expires.
The simplest database primitive that protects the invariant is usually the right choice.

complexity.note: Check affected rows to detect the losing write.
The second writer gets a duplicate error.
Set a timeout and a consistent lock order.

complexity.time: one read, one conditional write, then retry

complexity.note: Removes concurrency at the cost of latency.

commonMistakes: Reading a value, checking it in application code, and writing it back without an atomic guard.
Holding a transaction open across a network call to a payment provider.
Using a distributed lock without a fencing token and assuming the lease is a guarantee.
Choosing pessimistic locking everywhere and turning contention into connection-pool exhaustion.
interviewNotes: State the invariant first: no oversell, no double charge, no lost increment.
Name the database primitive that enforces it, not only the application check.
Say which isolation level you need and what happens when a transaction aborts.
Choose pessimistic or optimistic locking based on the expected conflict rate.
If you use a lease, explain how a paused holder is prevented from writing after expiry.

checkYourself.question: How does a conditional update prevent a lost update?
checkYourself.answer: The database evaluates the condition and changes the row under one lock. A second writer either waits and sees the new value or changes zero rows, so both writers cannot act on the same old value.

checkYourself.question: When is optimistic concurrency a poor fit?
checkYourself.answer: When conflicts are frequent. Many writers retry, waste work, and can create a retry storm, so a pessimistic lock or serialized queue may be better.

checkYourself.question: Why is a fencing token needed with a distributed lease?
checkYourself.answer: A holder can pause past its lease expiry and resume after another holder takes over. The token lets storage reject the stale holder's write.
